title_en: Exile Without Arrival: Displacement, Memory, and Time in Lamentations
abstract: Studies of forced migration frequently privilege movement: departure from a homeland, passage across space, and the construction of life elsewhere. Recent work on forced (im)mobility has complicated this model by attending to those compelled to remain amid conditions of violence. Lamentations pushes this complication further. Although the book names Judah’s exile, it does not follow the deported population to Babylon. Instead, its poems remain oriented toward Jerusalem, where geographical continuity masks the destruction of the relationships and practices through which place and communal time are produced. Bringing Lamentations into conversation with scholarship on displacement, relational place, migration temporality, and cultural memory, this essay argues that the book constructs displacement as the transformation of place and the rupture of temporal continuity through the interruption of cultic recurrence, the destruction of institutions’ ability to reproduce communal life, and the insecurity of inheritance and generational continuity. The poems formally stage the same disruption: memory preserves the world preceding catastrophe without making it recur, while lament, hope, and petition repeatedly open the present toward a possible future they cannot secure. “Exile without arrival” thus names Lamentations’ distinctive account of displacement: estrangement from a homeland that remains geographically present, from a past that remains available through memory, and from a future that can be imagined but not inhabited.

title_en: Gilbert Durand: Religion After Religion
abstract: This article has two principal aims. First, it seeks to provide a succinct account of the genesis and some of the fundamental concepts of Gilbert Durand’s (1921–2012) symbolic anthropology: the imaginary, sermo mythicus, the anthropological trajectory, and the transcendental fantastic. Together, these concepts constitute what we consider to be the horizon of his open epistemology. Second, this article seeks to underscore the contemporary relevance of this “science of the imaginary” or symbolic hermeneutics of culture: an understanding of homo religiosus as a condition of human existence that still has much to contribute to the contemporary study of religions and to understanding the spiritual crisis of the West in our post-secular age, gravely marked by the tendency toward neo-totalitarianism, technological reconversion, and an unprecedented ecological crisis.

title_en: Gnosticism as the Deep Structure of Modernity: A Philosophical-Anthropological and Political Analysis
authors: Melike Çelebi Özcan, Muhammet Caner Ilgaroğlu
abstract: This study examines modern humanity’s existential crisis and search for meaning from philosophical-anthropological and political perspectives by exploring structural parallels with ancient Gnostic cosmology. It argues that the existential void and chronic alienation arising from the dissolution of traditional theological frameworks cannot be adequately explained through purely sociological or empirical approaches. To illuminate the metaphysical dimensions of this crisis, the study brings Hegel’s, Marx’s, and Heidegger’s theories of alienation into dialogue with Eric Voegelin’s critique of the “Gnostic temptation” and the philosophical anthropology of Max Scheler, Arnold Gehlen, and Helmuth Plessner. Methodologically, it adopts a comparative-hermeneutic approach in which structural analysis serves as the primary comparative principle, while phenomenological analysis clarifies how alienation is experienced across different philosophical frameworks. Rather than positing historical, genealogical, or causal continuity between modernity and ancient Gnosticism, the study identifies structural correspondences in how human beings experience estrangement, interpret disorder, and imagine possibilities of liberation, reconciliation, or transformation. It argues that modern alienation exhibits a pattern analogous to the Gnostic myth of the soul’s estrangement within a flawed material world, while differing substantially in its ontological assumptions and responses. Thus, modernity reveals structural affinities with the Gnostic imagination without implying direct historical or doctrinal continuity.

title_en: The Temple Mount/Ḥaram al-Sharīf as a Space of Interreligious Coexistence and Tolerance During the Crusader Period, 1099–1187
abstract: This article examines the transformation of the Temple Mount/Ḥaram al-Sharīf from a scene of massacre and Christian appropriation in 1099 into a space of limited interreligious coexistence during the second half of the twelfth century. Drawing on Christian, Muslim, and Jewish travel accounts, it argues that, from the 1160s onward, the Franks permitted Jews and Muslims to enter the esplanade and worship there, while continuing to restrict their residence in Jerusalem. This change reflected a combination of Frankish acculturation in the Levant, economic pragmatism, and growing Byzantine influence under Manuel I Komnenos. Yet tolerance was selective and spatially differentiated. While non-Christians could pray on the Temple Mount/Ḥaram al-Sharīf, the Cave of the Patriarchs in Hebron was closed to them. The article therefore identifies a significant but bounded reorientation of Frankish policy toward non-Christian worship in Frankish holy sites.

title_en: Measures of Religiosity and Spirituality Used in Spanish-Speaking Health Contexts and Health Research and Their Conception of Religiosity/Spirituality: A Systematic Review
authors: David Almaraz, Jesús Saiz, Florentino Moreno Martín, Klaus Baumann
abstract: Research on religiosity and spirituality (R/S) in health is growing in Spain and other Spanish-speaking contexts, highlighting the need for reliable instruments reflecting diverse R/S conceptualizations. This systematic review aimed to identify, categorize, and critically evaluate Spanish-adapted measures used in health contexts and health research in Spain and Latin America, and to examine their underlying R/S conceptions. A systematic search of five databases was complemented by supplementary searches. A total of 98 studies were included, identifying 58 unique measures: 34 R/S-specific measures, 21 broader constructs with an explicit R/S dimension, and 3 professional spiritual-care measures. Measures covered heterogeneous domains, including spiritual well-being, spiritual experience and transcendence, religious beliefs and practices, relationship with God or the sacred, R/S coping, and R/S needs and distress. Psychometric evidence was uneven, with structural validity, internal consistency, and hypothesis testing/construct validity most frequently assessed. Nine measures had sufficient evidence for three or more measurement properties, 16 for two, 9 for one, and 24 for none. No measure met COSMIN category A criteria; 51 were classified as category B and 7 as category C. These findings underscore the need for careful instrument selection based on the construct, population, cultural context, and measurement evidence, and support further validation across diverse Spanish-speaking populations.

title_en: The Price of Perfection: Moral Enhancement, Free Will, and the Limits of Technological Salvation
abstract: In 2017, Elon Musk stated that humans must augment their mental capabilities through the “merger of biological intelligence and machine intelligence” lest they risk becoming “house cats” to artificial intelligence. In 2024, he successfully implanted his “Neuralink” chip in a human patient. Now, while the idea of improving the human condition by integrating technology into the human body did not begin with Elon Musk, his tangible advancements in neural implants have shifted the ethical questions surrounding them from theoretical to practical. One particularly thorny application of this technology—one that raises both ethical and existential questions—is its use for moral enhancement. Ethically, we must consider whether it is good or bad to employ technology that ensures individuals act morally. Existentially, if human free will is expressed most meaningfully through moral choice, should we be willing to relinquish that freedom for the sake of social harmony, crime prevention, even world peace? Or must we accept a world marked by moral failure, violence, and injustice in order to preserve human autonomy? To address these questions, I examine contemporary philosophical debates surrounding moral enhancement and place them in dialogue with classical Jewish sources. For, as will be shown, Jewish thought offers a unique framework for addressing both the ethical permissibility of moral enhancement and the existential tension between free will and moral perfection. By juxtaposing cutting-edge neurotechnology with ancient moral anthropology, this paper invites a reassessment of what it means to be human in an age increasingly capable of reshaping human agency itself.

title_en: Sacred Architecture as the Body of Memory: Material Religion and the Holy City of Mandarom Shambhasalem
abstract: This contribution analyzes the Holy City of Mandarom Shambhasalem in France as the material expression of the spiritual beliefs, memories, and narratives of a new religion, Aumism, a new syncretic religion labeled a sect by French authorities. Built since the end of the 1960s, this controversial place of worship has become a custodian of intangible heritage and the group’s collective memory, contributing to cultural diversity and the debate on society’s heritage. Religious architectures demonstrate that the symbolic use of materials and sacred buildings both reveal and conceal spiritual messages, giving material form to the immaterial. The study is based on a qualitative ethnographic approach, including media and audiovisual materials, natural documents, participant observation, and non-directive interviews. The study draws theoretically on the classical notion of collective memory, new studies of spatiality and religion, material religion, and studies on sacred spaces. The results show that the Holy City functions as a body of collective memory through three mechanisms: the collective construction by first-generation members; the incorporation of absence as active mnemonic sites; and the guided tour as a performative act of memory transmission. The discussion highlights how the unmaking of sacred space has paradoxically intensified its mnemonic power, and how the architecture of a contested new religion participates in broader social debates on heritage and cultural diversity.

title_en: The Theological Foundations of Fate in Early Stoicism
abstract: The early Stoics developed a theology in which divine providence governs the cosmos through fate. This article examines its foundations in natural philosophy, showing how the Stoics transformed Plato’s theological cosmology into an account of immanent divine governance. Plato’s Timaeus provided a starting point centred on divine craftsmanship and cosmic order, yet the Stoics rejected its incorporeal Forms and divine agency beyond becoming. Adopting corporealism, they understood god as a corporeal rational principle acting on matter from within. Three transformations are central. First, total blending replaces separation, explaining how divine reason pervades and sustains the cosmos. Second, the passive principle recasts the receptacle as a passive universal substrate, removing necessity as an independent material constraint on divine action. Third, the legislative model transforms divine craftsmanship into governance through universal and strict providential law. These transformations establish divine immanence through a route distinct from Aristotle’s natural teleology, centred on individual substances and their potentiality and actuality. They also clarify the religious significance of Stoic fate: the world’s causal order expresses the continuous activity of divine providence. Strict determinism thus emerges from an account of god’s all-encompassing governance of the cosmos.

title_en: From Local Worthy to Temple Exemplar: Yang Shi’s Enshrinement and the Ritual Making of Cheng–Zhu Orthodoxy
abstract: Studies of Yang Shi’s enshrinement in 1495 have traced the earlier petitions and examined how changing Ming criteria for admission to the Confucian temple shaped the outcome. This article asks a different question: how did a disputed intellectual genealogy acquire binding ritual authority? Reading local gazetteers, academy records, court chronicles, memorials and genealogical writings together, it argues that Yang’s canonization unfolded through a hierarchy of ritual recognition. Academy and local-worthy worship made him a durable regional exemplar; the court’s rejection of empire-wide enshrinement in 1465 nevertheless authorized a local shrine and thereby created an intermediate ritual status; later advocates recast him from an imperfect exegete into an indispensable transmitter and defender of the Way. Imperial enshrinement did not simply acknowledge an already settled Cheng–Zhu succession. It standardized one contested genealogy across state schools and made that genealogy publicly performable. Yang’s case thus shows how ritual hierarchy constituted Confucian orthodoxy through continuing sacrificial relations between living communities and exemplary predecessors.

title_en: Substance and Emptiness: A Comparative Study of the “Absolute Being” in Kant’s Philosophy of Religion and Tathāgatagarbha–Dharmakāya Thought in the Ratnagotravibhāga
abstract: This article compares the concept of the “Absolute Being” in Kant’s philosophy of religion with tathāgatagarbha–dharmakāya thought in the Ratnagotravibhāga, focusing on their conceptual forms and philosophical functions. In the theoretical reason, Kant restricts the most real being to a transcendental ideal of pure reason and permits only its regulative use; in the practical reason, Kant grants the idea of God the legitimacy of rational faith by treating it as a moral postulate. By contrast, the Ratnagotravibhāga uses dharmakāya, tathāgatagarbha, and buddha-nature to explain the ground of sentient beings’ attainment of Buddhahood, and develops an emphatically affirmative soteriological discourse through the four qualities of “permanence, bliss, self, and purity” and the nine similes. The article argues that the two are not substantially the same kind of “absolute”. Kant’s “Absolute Being” has only the status of an idea and a postulate: critical philosophy denies theoretical knowledge of it without removing the personal determinations of the practical idea of God. Tathāgatagarbha–dharmakāya, for its part, must be understood within the limits imposed by dependent origination, no-self, and twofold emptiness. Even so, the two display a limited but identifiable functional correspondence insofar as both mark the limits of cognition, sustain the meaning of practice, and contribute to systematic unity. By submitting each position to the reciprocal scrutiny of Madhyamaka emptiness and Kantian critique, the article further argues that this correspondence is illuminating only when their ontological, epistemological, and soteriological differences are fully acknowledged. The tension between substance and emptiness is therefore not an opposition that can simply be dissolved; it is an occasion on which two traditions can disclose one another’s theoretical presuppositions and boundaries.

title_en: Spiritual Lifestyle in Ibn ʿArabī’s Mystical Theology: Foundations and Practical Implications
abstract: Ibn ʿArabī (1165–1240 CE) is best known for his metaphysics; his teaching on how life should be lived has received less attention. Drawing on al-Futūḥāt al-Makkiyya and the Fuṣūṣ al-Ḥikam, this study asks how four of his central doctrines—the Oneness of Being (waḥdat al-wujūd), the Perfect Human (al-insān al-kāmil), Divine Self-disclosure (tajallī), and the Five Divine Presences (al-ḥaḍarāt al-khams)—bear on the organization of human life. It argues that together they carry specific practical consequences, traced along four dimensions: the epistemological, the ethical, the social, and the devotional. Ibn ʿArabī’s own distinction between the primary worship inherent in all beings and the secondary worship the Law prescribes states the resulting ordering of life in brief. Compared with the sociological accounts of lifestyle, his account differs at three points: where lifestyle for Weber marks social distinction, Ibn ʿArabī’s etiquette (adab) works against it; where Bourdieu grounds durable dispositions in social position, Ibn ʿArabī orients their formation toward the Divine Names; and where Giddens makes lifestyle the frame for religious practice, Ibn ʿArabī makes worship the ground of the rest of life. The result is not a generic spirituality but the ordering of a specifically Muslim life, anchored throughout in the Quran, the Sunna, and the Sharīʿa.

title_en: Developing Missional Fatherhood as a Faith-Based Model for Family Resilience Among Father-Absent Households in South Africa
authors: Fazel Ebrihiam Freeks, Willem Andries Nel
abstract: Father absence remains a persistent social problem in South Africa and is associated with significant pressures on family functioning, child development and community life. This article further develops Freeks’s concept of missional fatherhood as a faith-based model for strengthening family resilience among father-absent households in South Africa. The study employs an integrative literature review with qualitative thematic synthesis and a concept-development orientation. Missional fatherhood is grounded in the missio Dei and proceeds from the theological conviction that God is a missional and sending God. To understand the concept, mission must be understood in its deepest theological sense: God is the author of mission; God has sent and continues to send; Christ is central to this mission, and the Holy Spirit enables people to participate in the mission of the triune God. Consequently, missional fatherhood is people-oriented rather than institution-oriented or programme-focused. People participate in God’s mission by being sent towards other people, families and communities through responsible presence, sacrificial service, spiritual formation and restorative care. By placing Freeks’s concept in dialogue with missional theology, South African fatherhood scholarship, social fathering, family resilience, relational ecology and Ubuntu, the article further develops the concept as a broader theological and relational response to father absence without diminishing the responsibility of biological fathers. It argues that missional fatherhood offers a theological and relational contribution to addressing father absence by understanding fathering as missional praxis through which people participate in God’s continuing restorative work among families and communities.

title_en: Dangerous Relations: An Ethnographic Study of Leprosy, Ritual, and Social Order Among the Nuosu of Southwest China
abstract: In recent years, new animism has encouraged scholars to understand animist worlds as constituted through multiple relationships between humans and nonhumans. Danger, pollution, and asymmetry within these relationships, however, still need to be examined through specific ethnographic cases. Drawing on fieldwork conducted in Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture between December 2020 and February 2025, this article examines Nuosu understandings of leprosy, together with the everyday taboos, protective practices, and bimo rituals surrounding the disease. The ethnography shows that, in the Nuosu animist world, leprosy takes the forms of dangerous nonhuman agents known as “Cut” (ꋄ), “Nu” (ꆓ), and “Nuse” (ꆓꌋ), which can transform into one another. These beings move through natural objects, human bodies, kinship ties, and the ancestral realm. Their danger lies not only in the harm they cause to the body, but also in the way their pollution disrupts established boundaries between humans and nonhumans, the living and the ancestors, and lineage insiders and outsiders. The Nuosu seek to avoid and expel these dangerous beings, yet they cannot remove them once and for all because the beings are embedded in bodies, lineages, and relations with ancestors. This gives rise to a relational paradox: they must be rejected, but they must also be dealt with repeatedly. Taboos, protective practices, ritual expulsion, and the purification of ancestral spirits provide different means of managing this paradox, redrawing boundaries, and restoring order. On this basis, this article defines “dangerous relations” as nonreciprocal relations that people seek to sever but that repeatedly re-emerge through pollution, kinship, and ontological transformation. The Nuosu case shows that animist worlds encompass ethe formation and maintenance of relationships, as well as efforts to avoid or transform dangerous relations and manage the boundaries surrounding them.

title_en: Specular Mediation and Loingprès: A Symbolic Hermeneutics of the Imago Dei in Marguerite Porete
abstract: This article examines the symbolism of the mirror in Marguerite Porete’s Le Mirouer des simples ames and argues that the mirror does not function as an isolated metaphor of self-knowledge, but as the form of a mediation in which presence takes place through distance. Drawing on the French Chantilly manuscript, the study traces the unfolding of this structure from the initial portrait and the conception of the book as a gift from Love to its internalization in the three deaths and the seven states. Between these two moments, the dialogical composition and the distribution of agency articulate the passage from the received book to the transformed soul, while the medieval constellations of the amorous and transformative mirror situate its symbolic grammar historically. From the perspective of symbolic hermeneutics, the analysis shows that Reason and Love operate as opposed yet complementary mirrors, and that annihilation progressively displaces the initiative of vision until it reaches the formula “Dieu se voit de luy en elle, pour elle, sans elle” (“God sees Himself from Himself in her, for her, without her”). The imago Dei thereby acquires a relational meaning and designates a participatory likeness that preserves the difference between creature and Creator and makes distance the very medium of union.

title_en: Protecting Chan Through Regulations: The Storehouse Regulations of Gaomin Monastery and the Institutional Construction of Sacredness in Republican China
abstract: During the Republican period, many Chinese public monasteries relied on paid liturgical services 應酬經懺 (yingchou jingchan) for financial survival. Gaomin Monastery 高旻寺, under Chan Master Laiguo 來果妙樹, permanently refused such services, forgoing a readily available source of income. This article examines the institutional logic that sustained this refusal through a close reading of the Storehouse Regulations 庫房規約 (Kufang Guiyue), a monastic administrative document. Drawing on Berger’s theory of plausibility structures and his concepts of institutionalization, legitimation, and internalization, it develops five related dimensions of analysis: social foundations, institutional support, boundary maintenance, the reconstruction of meaning, and ritual practice. The article argues that stringent institutional administration provided the foundation for sustaining Gaomin Monastery’s sacred meaning system and that, under conditions of pluralism, such institutional rigor could help preserve the boundaries and integrity of sacredness. It offers insights into theories of religious strictness and the relationship between the sacred and external meanings in lived religion from an East Asian Chan perspective.

title_en: Devotion and Emotion: Moralized Joy in the Parma Hebrew Psalter
abstract: In the late thirteenth or early fourteenth century, Parma Psalter, a luxury, small format North Italian Hebrew codex, the depiction accompanying Psalm 149 features a strikingly rare scene: a tightly consolidated Jewish choir led by a gesticulating choirmaster. While previous scholarship has often mined this miniature for its empirical musicological evidence, this study employs methodologies from the history of emotions to decode the formal and conceptual strategies shaping the illumination. The inquiry analyzes the focalized truncation of the figures and their expressive emotional economy, and uncovers the parabolic inclusion of a female singer. The text addresses how the artist negotiated the theological problem of representing religious exultation, adhering to a prevailing mode of severe facial mimesis to signal rigorous spiritual governance over the carnality of joyful emotions. The resulting equilibrium of opposing values yields a visual oxymoron: close mouthed, austere choristers vocalizing a jubilant, eschatological psalmody. The study demonstrates that, by anchoring this performance in Jewish exegesis and paraliturgical nuptial customs, the illuminator refined and moralized an otherwise suspect sensation of joy into a legitimate, disciplined instrument of elevated private and communal devotion.

title_en: Defending Purpose Theory of Meaning: Meeting Koons’s New Euthyphro Dilemma
abstract: The recent surge of interest in the philosophical study of life’s meaning generated multiple challenges to a default, often taken-for-granted theistic position—Divine Purpose Theory (DPT). This paper defends DPT against Koons’s Euthyphro Dilemma (KED), which questions whether a purpose is meaningful because God assigned it or did God assign that purpose because it is meaningful. The first horn implies that God’s purpose is arbitrary, while the second horn renders God otiose in life’s meaning. Koons points out that the standard theistic response to KED fails because it generates asecond-order Euthyphro dilemma that remains unresolved. This paper first argues that we can resolve the second-order Euthyphro dilemma if we read Koons’s interlocutor—Alston—more charitably. Second, this paper shows how KED misses the target. While DPT is an account of life’s meaningfulness, KED is only about purposes’ meaningfulness. In addition, this paper also argues that KED, even as a challenge to an account of purposes’ meaningfulness, is a false dilemma. Last, this paper modifies KED into a version (Revised-KED) that specifically targets DPT as an account of life’s meaningfulness and argues that committing to the first horn of Revised-KED does not imply that God is arbitrary in God’s choice of purposes.

title_en: Printing the Americas for Catholic Europe: Jesuit Knowledge, Missionary Imagination, and Identity in the German-Speaking Lands, 1546–1800
abstract: This article examines how Jesuit and Jesuit-related printed writings about the Americas circulated in the German-speaking lands between 1546 and 1800 and how they mediated Catholic knowledge, missionary imagination, and claims to collective identity. Drawing on a representative, though not exhaustive, selection of German-language originals and translations—including letters, missionary reports, books, compilations, and periodicals—it combines diachronic textual analysis with the history of ideas. Rather than treating circulation as evidence of reception, the article examines how authors and editors represented American societies and missionary activity for their intended audiences. It identifies three overlapping phases. From the 1540s to the 1670s, narratives of suffering, martyrdom, and conversion represented the Americas as a theater of missionary sacrifice and reinforced Jesuit corporate and Catholic identity. From the 1670s to 1767, accounts of American customs, polities, and religions increasingly organized difference through hierarchies of civilization and offered a framework through which forms of German-speaking collective identity could be imagined. After 1767, and especially following the suppression of the Society in 1773, writings by former Jesuits and Jesuit-related authors became more defensive while also displaying greater internal differentiation. In this context, Creole writers defended the natural world and peoples of the Americas against claims of degeneracy, thereby giving greater visibility to their own claims to epistemic and cultural authority, whereas German-speaking former Jesuits placed greater emphasis on defending the legitimacy of the missionary enterprise. The article shows that these writings both transmitted knowledge about American realities and selectively organized that knowledge through Eurocentric assumptions. Across these phases, representations of Indigenous societies as requiring Christian and civilizational tutelage and of missionaries as agents of conversion, improvement, and social order provided a discursive framework through which missionary and colonial intervention could be presented as legitimate.

title_en: “Migration as Grace”: Brown Public Theologies of Migration
abstract: This article proposes the constructive theological principle of “migration as grace”. Throughout Scripture, we see that migration is a locus in which God intervenes and acts graciously on behalf of migrants. Based upon the practice of “telogia en conjunto” (“communal theological reflection”) drawn from Latina/o theology, the essay brings the author’s own constructive theological proposal of “migration as grace” in conversation with other Latina/o theologians, including Jorge Lara-Braud, Justo González, M. Daniel Carroll Rodas, Jacqueline Hidalgo, Efrain Agosto, Rodolfo Galvan Estrada III, Miguel Echevarria, Roberto Mata, Daniel Montañez, and Francisco Zamora Avila. Their theologies address key themes such as creation; exile; new exodus; migration as Scriptural primary narrative arc; and “enemies of the state and citizens of the Kingdom of God.” This essay argues that, since the 1970s, Latina/o theologians and pastors such as those under consideration have seen their own painful yet redemptive migration stories reflected in the Bible, and in turn developed diverse theologies of migration. These theologies, moreover, are part of a larger 500-year tradition of prophetic theological reflection which may be called Brown Theology. This article also draws upon patristic sources to demonstrate that Brown Theologies of migration have a solid foundation in the early church’s self-understanding as a community of sojourners. Finally, this essay places these Brown theological accounts in conversation with contemporary anti-immigrant rhetoric, white Christian nationalism, and recent United States immigration policies.

title_en: “Time and Position”, Cosmic Principle, and Delights in Heaven: Examining the View of Shengsi 生死 (Life and Death) in the Study of Yijing
abstract: The problem of shengsi 生死 (life and death) is one of the most fundamental and intractable questions of human existence, yet remarkably little systematic work has been done on the Yijing’s own conception of sheng 生 (life) and si 死 (death) as an integrated philosophical and religious problem. Drawing on the Yijing text, the later commentaries, and conceptual analysis, this study seeks to fill this gap by investigating the Yijing’s conception of sheng 生 (life) and si 死 (death) in its three basic structural perspectives: “time and position” (shi wei 時位), the cosmological alternation of yin and yang, and the existential posture of “delighting in Heaven” (le tian 樂天). The first perspective shows that sheng 生 (life) and si 死 (death) are situational states depending on one’s circumstance within changing configurations of time and position. The second perspective lifts this situational awareness to the level of cosmic principle: sheng 生 (life) being the union of yin and yang, si 死 (death) as their separation, both of which are necessary phases in the endless process of cosmic generation. The third perspective traces the process by which this cosmological understanding was internalized. It leads to an existential attitude of “delights in Heaven and knows his own fate and what Heaven bestows” (le tian zhi ming 樂天知命), a condition in which the fear of si 死 (death) is overcome by acceptance. In this case, the meaning of sheng 生 (life) and si 死 (death) is fulfilled in the realization and accomplishment of one’s “will” (zhi 志) and “nature” (xing 性) endowed by Heaven. The study concludes that the Yijing offers a philosophical and religious vision in which sheng 生 (life) and si 死 (death) are not opposed and separated, but integrated as complementary phases of a single, ongoing process of cosmic and human realization. It speaks to the perennial human question of how finite beings, conscious of their mortality, can find meaning and fulfilment in a world of constant change.

title_en: “The measure of your [thinking] is to me unknown:” Aḥmad Fāris al-Shidyāq’s Comparative Epistemology in “Maqāmah on Chapter Thirteen”
abstract: Aḥmad Fāris al-Shidyāq (1804/5–1887) was an unusual Arab renaissance figure whose work spanned travel and fictional writing, Bible criticism and translations, Arabic lexicography, poetry, philology, and grammar. His intellectual and professional life involved working with several languages, including Arabic, English, French, Hebrew, Syriac, Latin, and Maltese. He lived a life marked by political upheavals and intellectual polemics, prompting his multiple conversions across Maronite Christianity, Protestantism, and Islam. Although his work has received scholarly attention for its comparisons of Mediterranean and European societies, his own understanding of comparative practice remains understudied. This article seeks to reconstruct al-Shidyāq’s comparative epistemology by examining his fictional and non-fictional writings. It argues that his critique of the limits of comparison, and of analogical reasoning as they were practiced in the nineteenth century, emerged from a critical, anti-institutional stance toward three communities that marginalized embodied experience as a site of knowledge: the clergy in Lebanon, British orientalist philologists and translators, and American missionary translators. This article first situates al-Shidyāq’s work within nineteenth-century comparative thought and practice. It then combines close textual analysis with insights from translation and embodiment studies, cultural history, and the history of science and ideas to reconstruct al-Shidyāq’s distinct comparative method. A micro-analysis of al-Shidyāq’s first maqāmah will demonstrate how his comparative practice is ethically grounded in the dynamic interplay between formal and harmonic analogies.

title_en: Literature as Theological Heterology and Its Contribution to Liberation Theologies in the 21st Century: An Archaeo-Genealogical Approach Through a Brazilian Case Study
abstract: Within Latin American Liberation Theologies, socio-analytical mediation has been decisive for interpreting structures of domination, yet it does not exhaust the lived, affective, and symbolic dimensions through which subjects inhabit and transform those structures. This article examines how Theology and Literature can broaden the moment of seeing without replacing socio-political analysis. Methodologically, it combines Antônio Manzatto’s anthropological approach with an archaeo-genealogical analysis of theological knowledge inspired by Michel Foucault and Michel de Certeau. It argues that literature can function as theological heterology when alterity modifies theological language, its objects, and the position of the speaking subject. The analysis of Carlos Drummond de Andrade and Adélia Prado identifies two distinct movements: the critique of images of God associated with obedience, guilt, and the legitimation of suffering, and the emergence of corporeal, affectable, and solidaristic forms of subjectivation oriented towards the poor. The article concludes that literature does not substitute socio-analytical mediation but reveals its insufficiency when isolated from affect, imagination, memory, and subjectivation. By articulating genealogies of power and ethics, literary mediation can contribute to renewing the see–judge–act method within twenty-first-century Liberation Theologies.

title_en: Atheism and the meaning of life
abstract: The editors introduce the special issue on atheism and the meaning of life, providing an overview of its scope and a concise summary of the contributions included in the issue.

title_en: Beyond the Image: Xiang and the Changing Functions of Christian Images in Late Ming and Early Qing China
abstract: Studies of Christian images in late-Ming China have largely focused on the iconographic and stylistic adaptation of European pictorial models. This article shifts attention from pictorial transformation to the changing functions of images across different contexts of circulation and reception. Taking Johann Adam Schall von Bell’s Jincheng Shuxiang 進呈書像 (1640) as its central case, it examines the historical semantics of xiang 像, the book’s material organization of text and image, differences among its surviving copies, and Yang Guangxian’s later appropriation of its illustrations in the anti-Christian Budeyi 不得已. The analysis situates xiang within the overlapping vocabulary of late-Ming illustrated books rather than treating it as a self-contained theory of religious images. More importantly, the transmission from Jincheng Shuxiang to Budeyi demonstrates that pictorial recognizability and image function did not necessarily travel together. Christian pictorial material could remain recognizable while being redirected from devotional and didactic contexts into anti-Christian polemical argument, while textual and pictorial components could follow partially independent trajectories of transmission.

title_en: Bridging the Ineffable: James Legge’s Theological Association of the Tao with God in His Translation of the Tao Te Ching
abstract: While James Legge’s 19th-century translation of the Tao Te Ching played a foundational role in the work’s Western reception, his explicit association of “Tao” (道) with the Christian “God” has often been dismissed reductively as missionary bias. That reading misses something. Legge’s theological framing was less an imposition of his fulfillment theology, his fierce advocacy for “Shang-Ti” (上帝) in the late Qing “Term Question” debates, and the institutional demands of Max Müller’s Sacred Books of the East series. Drawing on Bourdieu’s concept of habitus, Lefevere’s theory of patronage, and close reading of Legge’s translated text and its paratext, the paper reconstructs the logic of a strategy that was, in its own terms, coherent. The Tao-God association distorted the naturalistic and embodied character of Taoist thought in ways that took decades to correct. But the same framework that distorted also canonized: without Legge’s theological repackaging, the Tao Te Ching might have remained what it was before his intervention—a curiosity at the margins of Victorian learning.

title_en: The Language of Generosity: Between Spinoza and Cervantes
abstract: In this essay, I flesh out the elements of what I call a literary Spinozism, a thoroughly immanentist metaphysical explanation of the writer’s activity and of the ontological status of the literary text. Based on a conjoined reading of the Ethics and the Theological-Political Treatise, three concepts will be developed to account for the ontology of the literary work: internal necessity, affective power and self-reflexivity. To examine this Spinozian view of literary production, I develop one case-study, Cervantes’ Don Quixote, with particular focus on the complementarity between the orality of the spoken word and the grandiloquence of Don Quixote. This choice of case-study, as I hope to show, is not arbitrary. Spinoza’s radical immanentist hermeneutics and Cervantes’ revolutionary literary project in the Quixote are two attempts to address one and the same problem which both thinkers inherit from Christian (Erasmian) humanism, namely the problem of generosity. I end by attempting to illustrate the three Spinozian concepts with reference to Jorge Luis Borges’ work on the Quixote.

title_en: Tajwīd as a Codified Discipline: An Analysis in Light of Avicenna’s Criteria for Science
abstract: Tajwīd was recognized as an ʿilm in classical Islamic scholarship, yet its epistemic status as a codified discipline has received comparatively little systematic examination. This study investigates whether tajwīd exhibits Avicenna’s structural criteria for science: a determinate subject matter (mawḍūʿ), foundational principles (mabādiʾ), and organized problems (masāʾil). The analysis finds that tajwīd takes the letters of the Qurʾān, insofar as they are realized in recitation, as its subject matter; rests on self-evident, inductive, transmitted, and normative principles; and organizes its problems around articulation points (makhārij), phonetic attributes (ṣifāt), phonetic interactions, including idghām, elongation (madd), pausing and resumption (waqf and ibtidāʾ), and recitational error (laḥn). Its aim is to preserve the transmitted verbal and recitational form of the Qurʾān and maintain the integrity between wording and meaning. Methodologically, the study employs qualitative conceptual and textual analysis conducted through a structural and functional analogical framework. It shows that tajwīd combines theoretical systematization with supervised practice through transmission, listening, recitation before a qualified teacher, repetition, and correction. This analysis contributes to existing scholarship by shifting attention from the individual rules and pedagogical transmission of tajwīd to its internal disciplinary architecture, and by showing how a transmission-based and practice-centered Qurʾānic discipline can be analyzed through a classical Islamic framework of scientific organization without being reduced to demonstrative science. The study concludes that tajwīd is not identical to a demonstrative science but can be characterized as a codified, normative, transmission-grounded, and practice-centered Qurʾānic discipline within the broader classical Islamic conception of ʿilm.

title_en: Illuminating Sacred Value: Indigenous Creativity and the Translation of Religious Value
abstract: This article examines how the commercial circulation of Indigenous Australian artefacts produces a structured encounter between sacred Indigenous value systems and secular economic frameworks. Drawing on case studies from Papunya Tula, tourist markets, Bali boomerangs, and auction practices, it analyses how works grounded in Dreaming narratives, collective custodianship, and relational responsibilities to Country are translated into commodities assessed through price, provenance, and aesthetic authenticity. Methods include historical analysis of shifting research paradigms, material culture analysis of certificates and intellectual property cases, and review of contemporary museum and tourism practices. Rather than focusing solely on commodification or cultural appropriation, this article examines the mechanisms through which Indigenous forms of value are translated into categories that become legible within museums, markets, and legal systems. The findings suggest that market institutions reward narrow expectations of ‘tradition,’ dislocate works from their custodial contexts, and reconfigure sacred potency as a sellable experience or object. This does not suggest that religious value is wholly displaced; rather, a major difficulty emerges in how it is rendered legible within market systems that operate according to different logics of value. By tracing these processes of translation, the article illuminates how religious value becomes visible, transformed, or obscured within neoliberal marketplaces, highlighting the ongoing ethical and epistemic tensions that arise when sacred creative practices encounter commercial environments.

title_en: Baptism and Anabaptism: Reconsidering Thomas Müntzer’s Identity in the Reformation
abstract: Baptism and the Eucharist were the two sacraments preserved by the Reformation, and divergent interpretations of them served as a key marker for differentiating the various Protestant confessions and the radical movements alike. This same criterion also shaped historians’ classification and understanding of individual theologians’ confessional positions during the era. Müntzer’s conception of baptism and its influence constitute the core issue in any examination of his identity, particularly the question of whether he was an Anabaptist, or his relationship with Anabaptism. To explore this question, it is necessary to consider several dimensions: the baptismal thought of the Zwickau Prophets, Müntzer’s own views on baptism and his liturgical practice, and his influence on contemporary Anabaptist leaders in Switzerland and in the German lands. Müntzer’s attitude toward baptism followed a trajectory of progressive radicalization; his thought on the Holy Spirit, combined with his thought on baptism, formed a Spirit–-baptism theology tinged with mysticism; Müntzer’s theology of baptism and his baptismal practice are distinct from each other and operate on two different levels. His impact on the early Anabaptist leaders extended beyond baptism to eschatology and social-revolutionary ideas, and he thus played a significant role in the development of Anabaptist thought and constituted a complex theological landscape in the early Reformation.

title_en: Buddhist Healing: Methods and Mechanisms—A Madhyamaka-Oriented Investigation
abstract: In Buddhist discourse, the path of healing often begins with awareness. Its crucial element, however, lies not in awareness alone, but in the direction toward which awareness is oriented and in the transformative process that follows from it. Ultimately, this process concerns how reality is understood. Madhyamaka thought takes cognition as its point of departure and emphasizes cognitive transformation as a means of reshaping the relationship between individuals and phenomena. Such transformation is not merely an exercise of psychological imagination; rather, it may bring about substantive changes in the structure of lived experience. Contemporary scientific research on psychological change, by contrast, largely relies on quantitative data and instrumental measurement, with its primary emphasis placed on neuroscience and psychology, whereas religious studies more commonly approaches such questions through textual interpretation and philosophical analysis. Each approach offers a distinct level of understanding. Nevertheless, the question of how religious thought may be translated into concrete and practically applicable methods remains in need of further exploration. Against this background, the present study takes healing as its central concern and examines, from within Buddhist theoretical frameworks, whether Buddhism may be understood as a mechanism of cognitive and existential transformation. Focusing on Chapter One of the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, it argues that Nāgārjuna’s critique of arising is not merely an analysis of causality, but also a deconstruction of the linguistic and conceptual assumptions through which causality and existence are reified. By exposing both the limitations of language and the tendency to mistake conceptual constructions for reality itself, Nāgārjuna opens a therapeutic pathway through which rigid patterns of attachment, conflict, and suffering may be transformed. Furthermore, as individuals gradually loosen their reified assumptions about the self, others, and conflict through insight into emptiness, rigid boundaries between self and other, as well as between friend and enemy, may likewise be reconsidered. Such cognitive transformation may, in turn, provide a possible foundation for equanimity, compassion, and more inclusive forms of ethical engagement.

title_en: God-Nature and the Walpurgisnacht Motif in Goethe’s Faust: Religious Continuity and Contestation in Literary Form
abstract: Goethe’s three Walpurgisnacht scenes in Faust are usually separated as demonic spectacle, satirical intermezzo, and classical phantasmagoria. Read together, they form a poetic sequence interpreted through Goethe’s conception of God-Nature (Gott-Natur), a non-systematic conception of divinity as immanent in living, metamorphic nature. The sequence moves from the expansion and interruption of demonic freedom on the Brocken, through a reconciliation of natural powers announced but withheld in “Walpurgis Night’s Dream,” to the attempted poetic return of God-Nature in the Greek Fabelreich. Religious and mythic traditions are not treated as evidence of an intact pagan cult; they supply historically contested symbolic materials that Goethe reshapes to examine modern subjectivity. The ballad “The First Walpurgis Night” clarifies how conflict over pagan natural festivity contributed to the motif’s demonic imagery, while the dramatic scenes transform mountain festivity, fairy comedy, sacred healing, divine genealogy, and metamorphosis into tests of Faust’s relation to limit. Greek soil revives him, but his desire for Helen turns participation into possession. The sequence thus stages religious continuity and contestation within literary form: inherited symbols remain available, yet their capacity to restore a divine-natural order depends on whether the modern subject can receive rather than master them.

title_en: Whose Growth? Reimagining Spiritual Formation as a Site of Social Justice in Theological Education
abstract: Theological education positions spiritual formation as the primary mechanism for cultivating ministerial identity, yet this process is rarely socially neutral. This conceptual article contends that formation paradigms grounded in individualised models of personal holiness can reproduce epistemological and structural injustice by abstracting the developing self from the socio-political conditions of power, oppression, and solidarity. Bringing theological anthropology into dialogue with critical pedagogy and mental health scholarship, the article examines how institutional formation agendas may construct an aesthetic of spiritual maturity that can function to suppress structural critique. Central to this analysis is the concept of Welwood’s Spiritual Bypassing “spiritual bypassing”: the avoidance of psychological needs through overspiritualisation, extended here as a heuristic for the institutional reframing of structural conditions as individual spiritual problems. The article illustrates three related operations of this logic: the spiritualisation of ministerial burnout; the reframing of structural exclusion as deficiency; and the unilateral conception of spiritual growth that risks pathologising distress and marginalising the embodied reality, epistemic standpoint, and theological contribution of those outside the normative. Justice-oriented theological formation requires a substantive paradigm shift. It proposes moving from a normative discourse of individualised growth, sometimes predicated on performance and conformity, toward a framework that recognises the body and mind as sites of theological labour and sites of potential resistance. Connecting the central pedagogical and spiritual question, “How does the student grow?”, with “Whose interests does formation serve?”, the article advances a constructive framework for theological education centred on systemic critique and prophetic witness, contributing to an emerging scholarship on inclusive and justice-seeking pedagogical practice.

title_en: Before Heaven Yet in Accord: Reexamining the xiantian 先天 (Ahead of Heaven) Doctrine in the Yijing and Its Commentarial Tradition
abstract: The concept of xiantian 先天 (“ahead of Heaven”) in the Yijing has long been interpreted either as a cosmological claim about the priority of cosmic principles or as an epistemological assertion about the sage’s capacity for foreknowledge, yet neither approach has systematically examined its internal philosophical structure. This study examines whether xiantian possesses a consistent logic connecting the cosmological, practical, and existential dimensions of the Yijing by distinguishing three interrelated dimensions and tracing their progressive development. The first dimension concerns Heaven’s priority to human beings. Within the dynamic structure of the Three Powers (sancai 三才) of Heaven, Earth, and humanity, human beings are always situated within the transformations of Heaven and Earth. Heaven is therefore prior to human beings in the generative, principial, and axiological senses, while this priority at the same time provides the conditions under which human participation in these transformations becomes possible. The second dimension concerns humanity’s acting ahead of Heaven. Through the cultivation practices of “refining the principles and entering into the numinous” (jingyi rushen 精義入神) and “exhausting the numinous and knowing transformation” (qiongshen zhihua 窮神知化), human beings transform this possibility of participation into the actual agency to understand and respond to change. The capacity for “knowing the incipient” (zhiji 知幾) further shows how such cultivated agency can manifest itself as temporal aheadness, enabling the sage to discern and respond to change before it has fully taken form. The third dimension concerns the ultimate transcendence of the distinction between xiantian and houtian 後天 (“after Heaven”) in the sage’s accomplished state. At this level, “acting ahead of Heaven” and “acting after Heaven” no longer constitute two opposing modes of action, since human agency has come fully into accord with the Dao of Heaven. These three dimensions together reveal a continuous movement from Heaven’s priority, through cultivated human agency, to the consummate accord between Heaven and human beings. Understood in this way, xiantian provides an important conceptual axis connecting cosmology, self-cultivation, and the realized relationship between Heaven and human beings in the Yijing.

title_en: Adaptive Reuse Strategies in European Christian Churches
authors: Magda Mària i Serrano, Alba Arboix-Alió, Sílvia Musquera i Felip
abstract: In Europe, Christian churches constitute a substantial part of listed heritage. These numerous liturgical spaces are highly significant to the image of cities and possess unquestionable spatial, material, environmental, and symbolic qualities, yet paradoxically society has progressively ceased to use them as religious practice has declined. For decades, a range of strategies have been applied that activate the potential of these underused religious spaces through a wide variety of other activities and uses. The objective of this article is to identify, select, and analyse a series of case studies from the second half of the twentieth century and the first decades of the twenty-first century in which what Richard Sennett defines as “dynamic repair” has been applied: an approach that considers the potential functions of a space with almost no physical modification, completing and correcting what is underused or has fallen into disuse in order to extend its useful life. The study presents a systematic taxonomy of examples of intervention in European sacred heritage within three adaptive reuse strategies—substitution, alternation, and coexistence of functions—which demonstrate how these liturgical spaces can be reused through minimal alterations. These low-impact interventions, combined with the management of uses and occupancy times, enhance the value of this heritage, which bears witness to Europe’s social and cultural identity, and help to keep it active and prevent its underuse, degradation, abandonment or demolition.

title_en: Knowledge Disjunction and Temporal Stratification: A Critical Examination of Buddhist Entries in the Compiled Edition of the Yuan History Bibliography
abstract: The Compiled Edition of the 元史藝文志輯本 (Bibliography of Chronicles of Yuan Dynasty edition), compiled by Luo Zhuyun 雒竹筠 and Li Xinqian 李新乾, represents the definitive modern reconstruction of the Yuan dynasty’s scattered literary corpus, synthesizing and correcting earlier Qing supplements. Moving beyond a simple catalog of errors, this study employs a critical historical epistemology to analyze the persistent inaccuracies within its Buddhist categories. It argues that these mistakes—including paleographic corruptions, misreadings of monastic institutions and anachronistic inclusions of Ming works—are not random oversights. Rather, they are systematic artifacts that reveal the inherent limitations of reconstructing a lost bibliographic tradition. These limitations manifest as a knowledge disjunction between later compilers and Yuan-specific socio-religious structures, and as temporal stratification, where later historical layers and scholarly contexts inadvertently permeate the reconstructed past. By examining these entries as a palimpsest—a composite text bearing traces of its own production—this paper demonstrates that the Compiled Edition is both an indispensable scholarly achievement and a historically mediated construct. The conclusion emphasizes the necessity of using this foundational reference work with source-critical awareness, understanding it as much for the insights it offers into Yuan textual history as for what it reveals about the perennial challenges of historical reconstruction itself.

title_en: How Heaven Becomes Normative: Yin–Yang, the Five Phases, and the Kingly Way in the Dong Zhongshu Tradition
abstract: This article asks how cosmic order is connected to the Kingly Way in Han shu materials concerning the historical Dong Zhongshu and relevant chapters of the received Chunqiu fanlu on Heaven–human relations, yin–yang, the Five Phases, and rulership. Reading the Han shu memorials alongside Dong’s criticism of Qin, this article reconstructs a political problem: how could a ruler whose commands stood at the center of a unified empire be judged by a standard beyond his own will? Admonitory disasters invite self-examination before ruin, while the seasons and yin–yang render Heaven’s authority relevant to ordinary government. Related Chunqiu fanlu chapters extend this evaluative direction into appointments, virtue and punishment, and the welfare of the people. This article tests the framework against disasters under good government, the absence of disasters, and misgovernment without timely warnings. Neither an event nor its absence settles political judgment without interpretation. Heaven’s authority can therefore challenge a ruler, but its application remains contestable and cannot guarantee political compliance; the same cosmic reasoning can also support social hierarchy. The argument distinguishes the historical memorials from the composite Chunqiu fanlu and identifies both the normative work and the unresolved interpretive burden of this moral cosmology.

title_en: Edo Period Japanese Annotated Translations of the Taishang Ganying Pian and East Asian Religious Syncretism
abstract: During the Edo period, the Chinese Daoist classic Taishang Ganying Pian 太上感應篇 attracted the attention of Japanese intellectuals, including Confucian scholars and monks, and spawned a number of Japanese annotated translations. When interpreting core Daoist concepts, Japanese translators retained the doctrinal essence of the original scripture and realized localized adaptation via folk metaphors, miracle efficacy narratives, and syncretism with indigenous kami. In terms of intellectual syncretism, the translators inherited the Chinese tradition of the “Three Teachings in one” 三教合一 and extended it into a distinctive configuration that integrated the Four Teachings: Confucianism, Buddhism, Daoism, and Shintō. In terms of practical moral education, despite their diverse backgrounds, these translators shared a core goal: popularizing this scripture to educate ordinary people, eliminating sectarian bias via syncretic thought, and supporting social governance with virtue-promoting ethics. The deep resonance between China and Japan in cosmology and self-cultivation provided the cultural foundation that facilitated the transmission and reinterpretation of this classic in Japan.

title_en: The Portuguese Visitandines and Domestic Remedies (Eighteenth Century)
abstract: The first Portuguese convent of the Order of the Visitation of Holy Mary was founded in Lisbon in 1784 by French and Portuguese nuns. The Visitandines rapidly compiled recipes relating to cookery, hygiene and beauty, pharmacopoeia, and household management. The result was the production of a collection comprising 174 recipes and two novenas, some considerably earlier in origin and others reflecting contemporary realities. Within this recipe collection, 36 preparations were intended to address health problems, representing 20.6 per cent of the total. The recipes were designed both for ingestion and for topical application, and the preparations were described as balms, broths, poultices, prescriptions, and remedies. They were intended to treat a wide range of ailments, including the healing of wounds, epistaxis (nosebleeds), various forms of pain, different types of fever, injuries, gout (arthritis caused by an excess of uric acid), hemorrhoids, intestinal worms, emaciation, ophthalmological disorders, pleurisy, ruptures (hernias), and coughs, among others. Until the eighteenth century, Europe as a whole shared similar dietary principles grounded in the writings of Hippocrates (460–379 BCE), Galen (c. 129–217), and Avicenna (c. 980–1037). This meant that cookery fulfilled the fundamental function of rendering foods digestible according to medical conceptions that had prevailed since Antiquity. The preservation of health was understood to depend upon a balance involving multiple factors, both internal and external to the individual. In light of this source, it becomes important to examine similarities and differences between the remedies compiled by the nuns of the Visitation of Holy Mary and contemporary pharmacopoeias, assessing the presence of food as medicine at a time when chemical pharmacy was already gaining prominence. Moreover, the recipe collection makes it possible to identify not only a variety of health concerns but also the incorporation of products originating from other continents, revealing the continual updating of pharmacological practice even within cloistered environments.

title_en: “Strangely Familiar”: Tolkien’s Notion of Fantasy, Creation, and the Anthropocentric in Tarkovsky’s Solaris
abstract: J. R. R. Tolkien’s notion of fantasy is intriguing and invites conversation with other art forms and theologies of art. For Tolkien, fantasy is the art of using one’s imagination to create a “secondary world”—or “sub-creation”—that has “‘the inner consistency of reality’” and that compels “secondary belief.” Fantasy has a uniquely generative power and stems from humans’ will and “right” to create as beings created in the image of God. Fantasy, for Tolkien, hence ought to be a strictly literary enterprise, as it is unable without much difficulty and contrivance to be adequately captured by visual and aural arts like stage drama. However, and as I aim to show, film is a visual and aural medium that can both challenge and expand on Tolkien’s contentions. Specifically, Tolkien’s claim that drama is “anthropocentric,” something that fantasy “need not be,” may be engaged, refracted, and re-envisioned by film. In the present analysis, I will use Andrei Tarkovsky’s Solaris (1972) as a lens for showing how film achieves this. I will argue that, from both a formal and thematic standpoint, Solaris effectively renders the human—or anthropocentric—as an inherently and theologically fantastical phenomenon.

title_en: Migration and the Logic of Reverse Mission
abstract: The rejection of ‘metatheology’ and an accompanying hostility toward the term mission within the very subject of missiology resonates with what has been described as the postmodern rejection of metanarratives. The influence of this intellectual climate on understandings of mission is evident in the widespread appropriation of Thomas Kuhn’s theory of paradigm shifts in a plethora of missiological texts. Despite this, non-Western cultures are shaped by distinct indigenous epistemologies, creating tensions when migrant Christians bring very different understandings of truth into Western contexts and churches. This raises important questions for the idea of ‘reverse mission’ advanced by Jehu Hanciles. In this essay, the concept of reverse mission will be re-examined. Focusing on Akan Christian migrants from Ghana ministering in Britain, this article uses an epistemological particularist framework in order to explore how their theological knowledge might be conveyed within a cultural setting shaped by postmodern understandings of truth.

title_en: Between Christian Hagiography and Chinese Reclusion: Reconstructing Religiousness Through the Hermit Figure in Hermann Hesse’s Early Works
abstract: This paper takes Hermann Hesse’s Drei Legenden aus der Thebais and Der Dichter as its central subjects of study, examining, through comparison with German medieval literature and classical Chinese reclusion poetry, how he reworks the hermit figure by drawing on and departing from the Christian hagiographic tradition and Chinese Daoist reclusive culture, thereby reconstructing religiousness. The study finds that Hesse neither follows the hagiographic practice of demonstrating holiness through miracles, nor replicates the Chinese literati’s withdrawal from official and worldly affairs, nor the transcendent imagination of becoming an immortal. Instead, Hesse replaces miracles with labor and external demonic threats with psychological desires, transforming the saint-like hermit into a modern individual grappling with genuine human struggles. At the same time, drawing on the structure of the Bildungsroman, he reshapes the Chinese master figure into a spiritual mentor who guides self-awareness rather than religious redemption. Hesse seeks to shift “Religiousness” from an institutionalized, theocentric faith toward a personalized, internalized, and nature-grounded spiritual experience, thereby suggesting a possible literary path for modern people to find spiritual refuge and self-integration amid crises of faith and a rupture of meaning.

title_en: Visual Symbols, the Consciousness of Daotong, and Sacrality: A Study of Wang Yangming’s Sage Portraits
abstract: Wang Yangming’s sage portraits functioned as material objects that transmitted Confucian orthodoxy (daotong 道統) and constructed sacrality through visual symbols, inscriptional texts, and ritual deployment. Drawing on material culture studies, this article examines the typological classification of Wang’s surviving portraits, the material presentation of their visual symbols, the discursive functions of inscriptions, and their roles in shrine worship. It argues that sacrality operated at three analytically distinct yet historically interconnected levels: semiotic, discursive, and practical. This study traces the social life of particular portraits as they circulated among private collections, academies, printed books, family spaces, and shrines, gaining, losing, and reacquiring varying degrees and modes of sacrality. Their sacrality emerged from ongoing interactions between objects and human actors, rather than inhering as a fixed, inherent attribute. The integration of image, inscription, and ritual reveals how Confucian sage portraits served as material media for advancing claims to orthodox lineage and constructing sacrality in late imperial China.

title_en: Redemption and the Church of St. John: Futurity and Narrative Philosophy from Schelling to Rosenzweig
abstract: This article attempts to sketch the conditions of ‘narrative philosophy’, an idea rooted in the philosophies of Friedrich Schelling and Franz Rosenzweig, insofar as it is both a historical philosophy and a messianic–eschatological utopianism. The two contradictory perspectives unite around the idea of narrativity and a shared idea of the future as incessantly deferred u-topos. The article examines Schelling’s late sketch of the ‘three ages of the church’ (Kirchenalter) and its origins in Schelling’s Ages of the World (Weltalter) project, before detailing Rosenzweig’s relationship to this philosophy, specifically his grafting of the triadic Kirchenalter into his own philosophy. The focus is on the structural affinity between Schelling and Rosenzweig, insofar as they both have established open-ended utopianism, or messianism, which lies concealed in their nonetheless ‘purely rational’ systems of philosophy. The article plots the course of the entanglement, while also bringing out the originality of the ‘narrative philosophical’ enterprise, which in both cases was never fully systematized. Schelling never completed—or else abandoned—the Weltalter, while Rosenzweig died young before he could expand his ‘New Thinking’ system, which was first introduced in the Star of Redemption (Stern der Erlösung). The article also attempts to show how this narrativity depends on both an aesthetic framework and a political vision.

title_en: The Law in Matthew’s Spirituality
abstract: By depending upon Deuteronomy, Matthew features Jesus as the obedient son who fulfilled the law. Unlike Moses, whose disobedience prevented him from leading Israel to obey the law and realize covenant blessings in the land, Jesus fulfilled the law, thereby restoring land and people. He embodied the covenant promise, “blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the land” (Matt. 5:5; 11:29), and the fulfillment of the prayer, “Thy kingdom come, thy will be done, in the land as it is in heaven” (6:10). By extending the mercy of God to those banned from worshipping God in his temple, the unclean were able to obey the law of Moses and offer the proper sacrifices (8:4). But the embodiment of obedience to the law of Moses was rejected by the priests. The only obedient son of Israel, Jesus now claims, “all things have been handed over to me by my father” (11:27). Jesus is the law that must be obeyed, his yoke defines covenant obedience. His law is neither land-locked nor ethnically bound. And so, the end of Matthew’s Gospel marks the end of Moses and the beginning of our spirituality, when the resurrected Lord with all authority in heaven and in the land commissions his disciples to teach his commandments beyond Israel, both land and people. For Matthew, then, faithful obedience to Christ reveals the fulfillment of the law of Moses.

title_en: Retrieving “Natural Religion” in Aquinas: Giving Religion Its Due in the Theology of Religions
abstract: This study reintroduces the Christian theology of religions to Thomas Aquinas’s understanding of religion as an acquired moral virtue. Aquinas’s treatment of religion as a moral virtue challenges the norm of revelation-centric theological methods across the positional spectrum. The category of natural religion and a religiosity acquired through reason has been cited either as a negative contrast for supernatural theologies of universal religious origins, or utilized in support of apologetical arguments to promote Christian uniqueness. This study, on the other hand, will retrieve Aquinas on natural religion in order to support appropriate autonomy in theological discourse about other religions. Following a review of problematics in theological method in the theology of religions and a consideration of recent, salient scholarship on Aquinas and religion, the argument will turn toward an exposition of religion in the Secunda Secundae. A retrieval of Aquinas’s theory of acquired religious virtue highlights the corrective meaning of appropriate autonomy in natural religion as a strategy for doing rhetorical justice to the reality of universal religious acts, and as a metaphor for the exigent task of a theology of religions that does not absorb religion into a supernatural monism. The relevance of this study for practical theology will be considered in the concluding section.

title_en: The Extension and Rejection of Self-Cognition in the Saṃdhinirmocana-Sūtra: A Study of Self-Cognition in Pre-Dignāga Yogācāra Under the Scope of the No-Cognition Sentence
abstract: While contemporary scholarship has extensively focused on self-cognition in Dignāga and post-Dignāga Yogācāra traditions, early Yogācāra discussions of this theme remain comparatively understudied. Focusing primarily on the Vijñaptimātra Passage of the Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra (SNS) and secondarily on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha (MSA), this paper advances three core arguments. First, the vijñaptimātra theory substantially broadens the scope of self-cognition by integrating inner object-directed cognitive activities into its framework, establishing what this paper terms the “broad sense of self-cognition.” In contrast to the Vaibhāṣika’s Outside-Model (OM), which separates object-directed cognition from self-cognition, the vijñaptimātra framework establishes an alternative Inside-Model (IM) of cognitive operation. The IM further accommodates a narrower form of self-cognition alongside its broad counterpart. Accordingly, the vijñaptimātra doctrine fundamentally reorganizes the classical structure of self-cognition theory. Second, the SNS advances a radical “no-cognition sentence” that universally negates all cognitive activities and thereby rejects this expanded mode of self-cognition. Nevertheless, this radical stance generates several textual tensions and theoretical contradictions, which undermine its validity. Third, the MSA rephrases the no-cognition sentence by using the verb “grasp.” By integrating the trisvabhāva (three natures) doctrine with vijñaptimātra, this new expression restricts the scope of negation exclusively to cognitive activities grounded in the parikalpita-svabhāva (mere illusory nature), while validating cognitive operations pertaining to the paratantra-svabhāva (dependent nature). Meanwhile, according to the IM, these cognitive operations precisely constitute broad-sense self-cognition. Accordingly, through a comparative analysis of these two divergent expressions of the no-cognition sentence, this paper elucidates the doctrinal shift between SNS and MSA attitudes toward expanded self-cognition.

title_en: Protecting Ritual Identity: Inter-Ritual Issues in the Contemporary Practice of the Dicastery for the Eastern Churches
abstract: The article examines the contemporary practice of the Dicastery for the Eastern Churches concerning selected inter-ritual issues, with a focus on protecting the distinctive ritual identity of Eastern Catholic Churches. The analysis is based on the Dicastery’s document of 22 November 2024, which systematizes the policy of the Apostolic See relating to the indults of bi-ritualism, adaptation of rite, and transfer to another Church sui iuris. The aim of the article is to answer the question of how the contemporary practice concerning inter-ritual relations implements the principle of protecting ritual identity amid increasing mobility of both the lay faithful and clergy, and in Catholic communities that function in multi-ritual environments. The study employs a dogmatic-legal method and institutional analysis, drawing on the provisions of the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (CCEO), selected provisions of the 1983 Code of Canon Law (CIC/1983), the teaching of the Second Vatican Council, and the current practice of the Apostolic See. The analysis demonstrates that the provisions concerning bi-ritualism, adaptation of rite, and transfers of ascription (within the Catholic Church) do not serve merely an administrative function, but also form part of a coherent policy aimed at preserving the liturgical, theological, spiritual, and disciplinary heritage of Eastern Catholic Churches. The Dicastery’s practice is marked by a continuing tension between the protection of distinct traditions of these Churches and individual expectations of the faithful and clergy living in inter-ritual communities. The article demonstrates that the current canon law provisions on relations among Churches sui iuris serve not only to regulate jurisdictional and pastoral matters but also to safeguard the distinct ritual identity of those Churches and ensure the continuity of Eastern traditions in the face of globalization, Latinization, and the expansion of diaspora communities.

title_en: The Activity and Stillness of Taiji 太極: Metaphysical Construction and Divergences of the Yijing Cosmology in Song–Ming Neo-Confucianism
abstract: The question of activity and stillness (dongjing 動靜) is central to Song–Ming interpretations of the Yijing. Zhou Dunyi’s Taijitu shuo 太極圖說 established the basic framework of Confucian cosmology with the proposition that “Taiji in activity generates yang 陽; in stillness it generates yin 陰.” Yet this concise formulation left some interpretive problems. First, do activity and stillness pertain to the substance of Taiji itself, or only to yin and yang? Second, how can the cosmological principle that “(activity and stillness) each is the basis of the other” be reconciled with the self-cultivation imperative to “emphasizing stillness” (zhu jing 主靜)? The divergent responses of Zhu Xi and Wang Yangming to these questions reveal their different understandings towards the substance of Dao and the practice of self-cultivation. Working within a strict li 理- qi 氣 dichotomy, Zhu Xi identifies Taiji with li and insists that “li cannot be discussed in terms of activity or stillness,” thereby relegating these to the domain of qi. Clarification of the substance–function relationship further shows that three seemingly plausible readings, “Taiji as substance, activity and stillness as function”; “stillness as the substance of Taiji, activity as its function”; and “yang-activity precedes yin-stillness”, all miss Zhu Xi’s actual position. Furthermore, although Zhu’s program of self-cultivation centers on “emphasizing reverence” (zhu jing 主敬), stressing the mutual issuance of activity and stillness, it nonetheless retains a latent preference for stillness, thereby leaving an unresolved tension in his system. Wang Yangming responds to precisely this tension by reinterpreting Taiji through the heart-mind as substance, absorbing the generative principle of Taiji into the self-activating nature of the heart-mind itself. In self-cultivation, he replaces “emphasizing stillness” with the ideal of “being settled whether in activity or in stillness,” insisting on the interpenetration of activity and stillness. Their interpretations of Taiji thus reflect a crucial distinction between li-based and xin-based paradigms in the history of Yijing scholarship.

title_en: John Wesley’s Holistic Healing and Contemporary Cognitive Behavioral Therapy: Toward a Differentiated Integration
abstract: This study argues that contemporary CBT/RCBT and John Wesley’s theology of holistic healing reveal significant structural analogies despite their fundamental differences in agency, practices, and the goal of healing. This study first examines how each tradition understands the possibility and process of human change, as it compares CBT/RCBT’s views of therapeutic learning, cognitive reorientation, core-belief transformation, and individualized development with Wesley’s ideas of prevenient grace, repentance, faith and new birth, and sanctification.
