It then turns to the behavioral and relational practices for achieving transformation, as it delves into the analogical relation between CBT/RCBT’s emphasis on behavioral experiments and therapeutic collaboration and Wesley’s concern for the means of grace and social holiness. Finally, it considers the goal and scope of healing, as it relates adaptive functioning and whole-person flourishing in CBT/RCBT to Wesley’s vision of restoration in the image of God, holy love, and happiness in God. In that respect, the study proposes a model of differentiated integration, which suggests that Wesley’s theology harmonizes with CBT/RCBT’s therapeutic approaches for their structural similarities despite their different visions of agency, practices, and the goal of healing.

title_en: The Vegetality of the Symbol
abstract: This essay advances the hypothesis that the symbol has a vegetal mode of being, and, concomitantly, that plant life is itself irreducibly symbolic. Bringing the hermeneutic tradition of Gadamer, Ricoeur, and Ortiz-Osés into dialogue with Cassirer’s philosophy of symbolic forms, we argue that the symbol occupies a paradoxical space between presence and absence, clarity and mystery, the visible and the invisible—a tension it can never resolve without collapsing into either sign or concept. This structural indeterminacy is then fleshed out through vegetal figures: the seed, understood as a concrete, non-guaranteed promise of genesis that must “die” to bear fruit, and the meristem, whose undifferentiated tissue generates novelty from within an ongoing relation to its environment. Engaging biosemiotics, this study affirms that interpretation is coextensive with life itself, while criticizing biosemiotic accounts that dissolve meaning in biochemical signals and operations of coding and decoding, thereby losing the figural and spatial density proper to the symbol. Figures such as Hermes—a god of passages, of communication, and of hermeneutics—together with the notions of symbiosis, plasticity, and kintsugi, extend the analogy: both symbol and plant grow out of rupture and incompletion, articulating rather than fusing opposites such as life and death, or the sensible and the intelligible. Attending to the vegetal, plastic character of symbolic meaning opens a fruitful field of possibilities for engagement with interpretation, culture, and the more-than-human dimensions of thought.

title_en: Ontological Aspect Shift: Rethinking Maimonides’ Thirteen Principles as Existential Structures of Being-in-Creation
abstract: Debates over Maimonides’ Thirteen Principles (Ikkarim) have examined their doctrinal authority and contested reception. This article asks how their truth claims belong to halakhic existence. Its theoretical framework treats nature and creation as ontological determinations of worldhood constituted and stabilized through practice. Drawing on Wittgenstein’s aspect-seeing and phenomenological accounts of worldhood, it defines an Ontological Aspect Shift as a transformation in how the same empirical reality is disclosed and inhabited. Applying this framework through analyses of Maimonides’ primary texts and rabbinic sources, the article interprets the Ikkarim as theological formulations of the existential structures of being-in-creation. Halakhic practice constitutes this worldhood; doctrine articulates its structures through claims concerning transcendence, revelation, judgment, and fulfillment. The argument distinguishes the normative priority of command, the constitutive primacy of practice, and the explicative and critical function of doctrine. Emunah is reconstructed as enacted receptivity while its cognitive uses retain their validity. This account concerns worldhood without making theological truth a product of practice. Its contribution is to explain how doctrinal affirmation participates in constituting and critically articulating a commanded way of inhabiting the world. The reading preserves Maimonides’ doctrinal demands while advancing an interpretation of their existential function that he does not himself formulate.

title_en: The Last Sartre: a Dawning at Dusk
The Making of a Messianic Reality in the Iberian Peninsula After the Persecutions of 1391
abstract: This article reexamines the evidence for the messianic agitation that emerged in the Iberian Peninsula in the aftermath of the persecutions of 1391. Historians have generally treated the surviving Hebrew accounts as evidence for a messianic movement centered on a prophet or messianic figure named Moses, who allegedly appeared in Cisneros in Castile in 1392–1393. Modern scholarship has also attributed to Hasdai Crescas an active role in the dissemination of the messianic expectations associated with these reports. A critical reconsideration of the Hebrew sources, together with Joshua Halorki’s testimony, Pablo de Santa María’s omission of the Cisneros episode, and a newly discovered letter concerning the events in Cisneros, preserved in a Cairo Genizah manuscript, suggests a more complex picture. The article distinguishes between the demonstrable atmosphere of heightened messianic expectation among Jews and conversos and the historicity of a discrete messianic movement centered on an identifiable claimant. The newly discovered letter provides further evidence for the circulation of reports concerning Cisneros and for the process by which they became associated with Crescas’s authority. The article argues that Crescas’s role has been overstated and that the surviving narratives are better understood as products of a Mediterranean process in which rumors circulated through letters, acquired authority through attribution, and were progressively interpreted, rationalized, and textualized. The “Messiah of Cisneros” thus emerges not necessarily as a recoverable historical individual, but as a historical product of communication and collective imagination in the profound social and religious crisis that followed 1391.

title_en: Materializing Salvation: Toward an Eco-Things Theology of Ta Panta
abstract: This article centers on Jürgen Moltmann’s pneumatological understanding of creation and engages in critical dialogue with new materialism—specifically Karen Barad’s concept of intra-action and Bruno Latour’s political ecology, both of which emphasize the agency and activity of matter itself—in order to reconstruct an eco-things theology that illuminates the process by which ta panta (τὰ πάντα, ‘all things’) in Colossians undergoes what is here called ‘materializing salvation.’ The long history of matter’s exclusion within the theological tradition reached its culmination in modern theology’s otherworldly soteriology, which effectively relegated matter to the margins of the salvific drama. Today, rapid technological development and the deepening climate crisis call for a renewed theological recognition of the significance of matter and things, particularly in confronting the discourses that separate technology from ecology. Moltmann’s pneumatological ontology provides rich resources for responding to this call. By connecting Moltmann’s doctrine of creation with Paul’s ta panta (Col. 1:15–20) and the ‘groaning creation’ (Rom. 8:19–23), this article argues that ‘materializing salvation’ names the transformation of already-entangled relations toward the reconciliation and liberation of all things through the mutual indwelling of divine, human, and nonhuman agency. Entanglement as such is therefore not identified with salvation; entangled relations may also become exploitative, extractive, and death-dealing. Through this reconstruction, I propose an eco-things theology as a theology of materializing salvation.

title_en: From the Finite to the Infinite: A Comparative Study of the Systematic Thought of Nicholas of Cusa and Zhuangzi
abstract: Although Nicholas of Cusa and Zhuangzi belong, respectively, to the traditions of Christian theology and Chinese Daoist thought, systematic comparisons of their philosophies within a shared framework of human finitude and the pursuit of transcendence remain relatively scarce. Both take reflection on the limits of human cognition and on “ignorance” as the point of departure for their thought, and both situate the oppositions of finite experience within broader accounts of order. Zhuangzi, however, presents the Dao (道, “the Way”) as immanent in the generation and transformation of the myriad things, with infinity understood here in terms of their inexhaustible transformations. Cusa, by contrast, understands God as the absolute infinite and the transcendent source of creation. Their differing conceptions of infinity in turn give rise to two distinct paths of spiritual practice. Zhuangzi emphasizes loosening attachment to the fixed preconceptions of the mind through such practices of self-cultivation as “fasting of the mind” (xīnzhāi, 心齋) and “sitting in forgetfulness” (zuòwàng, 坐忘), thereby bringing the individual into accord with the Dao immanent in all things. Cusa, by contrast, emphasizes an unceasing approximation to truth through comparison, mathematics, and intellect, while maintaining humility by acknowledging the ontological distinction between creature and Creator. This article argues that the two thinkers converge in their critique of human epistemic arrogance but differ fundamentally over the ontological status of the infinite: Zhuangzi’s Dao is interpreted here as the immanent ground of the transformations of all things, whereas Cusa’s God is the absolute source transcending creation. This distinction ultimately gives rise to two different models of spiritual transformation: the former achieves integration with the natural order by loosening attachment to fixed distinctions, whereas the latter approaches the divine infinite through the continual pursuit of truth.

title_en: Evil as attempted closure: Kierkegaard on selfhood, freedom, and faith
journal: International Journal for Philosophy of Religion

title_en: The Immortality of the Soul According to Thomas Aquinas
abstract: This article systematically examines the question of the human soul’s immortality—or incorruptibility—in the writings of Thomas Aquinas. The study traces Aquinas’s three-stage argumentation across his academic career, distinguishing his approach from those of Plato, Aristotle, and later thinkers. The first stage highlights the immateriality of human intellection, deduced empirically from the soul’s capacity to know all corporeal forms and to abstract universals. Moving to the metaphysical plane, as a second stage, the analysis underscores the principle that a proper immaterial operation necessitates a corresponding immaterial esse (act of being); this distinct existence, Aquinas contends, is grounded in divine creation rather than natural pre-existence or an emanation from a universal soul. Finally, the paper details how Aquinas resolves the tension of the human psycho-somatic unity. The article clarifies that as a subsistent immaterial form, the soul is incorruptible per se, even upon the body’s demise. Furthermore, the article briefly assesses various historical and practical objections regarding the separated soul’s impoverished activity and individuation without matter. Ultimately, the text maintains that Aquinas’s nuanced philosophical defense takes the reality of death seriously and deliberately avoids Platonic dualism. This approach, it posits, serves as a reasoned “preamble to hope” that rationally complements the Christian doctrine of bodily resurrection rather than substituting it.

title_en: Transloyalties and the Construction of Martyrdom: Re-Reading Manche Masemola in Colonial South Africa
abstract: Missionary encounters in colonial Africa generated competing understandings of loyalty, citizenship, and belonging as Indigenous communities and Christian missions advanced different moral, educational, and religious visions of society. Although Manche Masemola has been widely commemorated within Anglican tradition as a Christian martyr, scholarship has largely interpreted her life through theological frameworks that privilege singular religious loyalty, paying limited attention to the competing Indigenous epistemologies and overlapping allegiances that shaped both her lived experience and historical memory. Drawing on the emerging concept of transloyalties, this article reinterprets the narrative of Manche Masemola by examining how Indigenous, familial, educational, religious, and colonial loyalties intersected in colonial Sekhukhuneland. It argues that martyrdom is not a fixed historical category, but a historically situated narrative constructed through competing understandings of loyalty, citizenship, and belonging. Rather than presenting Manche’s life as a binary choice between Christianity and Indigenous tradition, this article demonstrates how she navigated multiple moral communities whose competing claims became increasingly irreconcilable within the colonial encounter. By extending the concept of transloyalties beyond migration studies to colonial religious encounters, this article contributes to scholarship on martyrdom, missionary Christianity, colonial history, Indigenous knowledge systems, and citizenship education while offering a new framework for understanding how competing epistemologies shape historical memory and the construction of martyrdom narratives.

title_en: Global South Theology as Theological and Missiological Imperative: Decolonising Christian Theological Discourse
abstract: As of 2025, approximately 69% of the world’s 2.64 billion Christians reside in the Global South, Africa, Asia, and Latin America, yet theological education and academic discourse remain anchored in Eurocentric epistemologies. This article addresses that gap through a constructive theological synthesis integrating demographic, postcolonial, missiological, and ecclesial evidence. It advances a four-pillar argument for the necessity of Global South theology: (1) demographic representativeness, grounded theologically in catholicity and the missio Dei; (2) the historical imperative of decolonising theological discourse; (3) the theological richness of contextualised integral mission; and (4) the sociopolitical demand for a theology responsive to poverty, injustice, and cultural identity in the majority world. The article engages three scholarly objections, syncretism, Marxist reductionism, and theological relativism, and concludes with four recommendations for theological education reform, each explicitly anchored to one of the four pillars. The argument is not majoritarian; rather, it rests on the claim that Christian catholicity and the doctrine of the incarnation require the full theological witness of the global body of Christ.

title_en: The Receptive Act: Theorizing the Addressee in Divine Discourse Through Tafaʾʾul Morphology
authors: Hande Nur Bozbuğa, Zeynep Sayın, Yunus Bozbuğa
abstract: This article argues that, although recent work in speech act theory has increasingly engaged with uptake, reception, and the addressee’s participation, the addressee has not yet been sufficiently theorized as performing a distinct volitional and transformative act. Existing accounts illuminate important aspects of how an addressee recognizes, receives, or responds to an address, but they do not fully specify the intentional structure involved in actively appropriating its normative force. To address this issue, the article introduces the concept of the receptive act, understood as the addressee’s intentional enactment of this appropriation, and develops the concept of the hearer’s intentionality as the intentional structure through which this act is performed. The Arabic tafaʾʾul pattern, particularly its takalluf dimension, is employed not as a direct linguistic equivalent of a speech act category but as a linguistic resource for articulating this volitional structure: takalluf denotes deliberate and effortful striving toward a quality or state not yet possessed. The article therefore distinguishes the receptive act from uptake, receptivity, or perlocutionary effect by focusing on the addressee’s active appropriation of an address and its normative implications. In the context of divine discourse, to which Wolterstorff applied speech act theory, this approach provides a framework for examining how divine address becomes operative through the addressee’s intentional participation. The article concludes by proposing that the receptive act can be understood as a distinct, addressee-side dimension of speech act performance, complementing rather than replacing Austin’s tripartite framework.

title_en: “The Lord Had Closed up Her Womb”: Interpreting 1 Samuel 1:5c in the Context of the Infertility Narrative in Nigeria
abstract: The notion of God closing Hannah’s womb is represented in Nigeria, as in Africa at large, in the belief that infertility is a curse from the gods. Employing historical criticism, narrative reading, and the descriptive method, the article critically examined this notion, appraising its possible influence on the infertility narrative in Nigeria. It found that in OT tradition, the idea of God opening and closing women’s wombs connotes God’s prerogative to give or not to give children. While Yahweh gave children as a blessing to some women, those who could not conceive were believed by some to be under a curse from him. This article, however, found that the tradition that barrenness was divine punishment arose from the lack of biological knowledge about conception; hence infertility, like every other ailment, was attributed to God. Unfortunately, this belief has been inherited along with Christianity in most places, including Nigeria. Hence, in Nigerian churches, particularly the Pentecostal denominations, the healing of infertility is informed by the belief that it is caused by spiritual forces, and they do not believe that it can be God’s purpose for some people not to bear children. To this end, this article offered an alternative approach to infertility healing, which is based on the fact that the idea of infertility as divine punishment is scientifically false. In other words, some women are infertile due to certain natural causes. The marriage theology in Nigeria has to accept and begin to reflect this reality.

title_en: Moving Beyond Text: Rethinking Audiovisual Method in the Study of Lived Religion
abstract: While there is growing recognition of film’s role in shaping and illustrating beliefs—especially narratively and artistically—there remains limited academic engagement within religious studies practically working with audiovisual content more generally. This article attempts to address this gap by reflecting on the process of our own work on the short documentary film, Wild Swimming: A Liquid Devotion. In particular, we focus on the methodological and epistemological insights garnered from working this way and reflect on the questions it forced us to confront. The short film was made by the authors in 2024 and explores wild swimming as a contemporary implicit lived religious practice—instead of merely a physical activity involving cold-water immersion. The film attempts to show how it can serve asa pathway toward encountering the sacred. Reflecting on the experience of making the film, the paper explores what the medium can contribute to the ‘empirical excess’ of lived religious subjectivities—particularly the dimensions that are physically encountered and observed in practice, and how audiovisual content might be more fully integrated into the academic study of religion. Specifically, drawing from our experience of making the film, it argues for the value of audiovisual research in exploring the embodied experience, sensory encounter and spatial or environmental ritual as essential components of spiritual world-making. Central to this is an argument for the relationship between documentary film and the ethnographic study of lived implicit religion, especially with its focus on praxis Documentary conventions, we argue, align closely with approaches to lived religion that privilege lived subjectivities, embodiment and subtlety. These conventions allow film to show rather than tell and, importantly, to invite multiple and even unexpected readings. The paper argues that this is especially significant for the study of religion, which deals with realms that often exist outside descriptions in words, because audiovisual media expand the dimensions of communication available to us. Our intention is, therefore, not to privilege audiovisual methods over textual ones, but to consider what additional possibilities they may offer for understanding lived forms of religious practice. It allows for an expansion beyond written textual approaches which, despite the shifts in scholarship to focus on the body and material practice, still dominate the field. By highlighting several of the practical choices made in producing the film, the article also offers important points of reflection on how the experience of the sacred might be further conceived in this way and suggests avenues of focus for deepening audiovisual research within religious studies scholarship. It should be made explicit that the primary objective of this article is to advance a theoretical and methodological discussion of camera-based research for religious studies. Rather than offering an exhaustive analysis of the film itself, we use the film as an empirical case through which to interrogate broader methodological and conceptual questions. Given the constraints of the article’s length, a comprehensive film analysis lies beyond its scope. Instead, the film functions as the principal case study that enables us to develop, illustrate, and critically reflect upon the epistemological and methodological framework proposed in this article.

title_en: Women in Pastoral Christian Ministry: Inclusionary Practices
authors: Geneece L. Goertzen, Gaynor I. Yancey, Helen Harris, Mallory Herridge
abstract: Matters of equity regarding women, immigration, race, and identity have found Christian groups and houses of worship too often on the side of exclusion, yet sometimes joined with advocacy and affirmation. This article explores the notion that women in Christian pastoral ministry have been associated with increased focus on LGBTQ+ inclusion in the church. This notion is often framed negatively as an accusation among those who desire to keep women out of ministry settings. Following a literature review, the authors discuss this asserted connection between American clergywomen and commitments to justice across multiple marginalized groups. This discussion is based on evidence from an empirical qualitative research study on congregational discernment and inclusionary practices with marginalized populations. One of the unexpected results revealed that female-led congregations across time have engaged in advocacy by responding to social injustices like racism, poverty, hunger, homelessness, and equity. For clergy in this study, LGBTQ+ inclusion is simply an indication of love of God and neighbor, as in other injustices. This article extends the understanding of roles and purpose for American Christian women in pastoral ministry with a particular focus on response to marginalized culture. In their discussion, the authors posit that the promotion of dignity and welcome for all is about following the call of Jesus and serving those who seek the church for help and healing.

title_en: Testing Seventeen Centuries of Claims: An Ecologically Valid Multi-Method Empirical Study of Basilica-Plan Sacred Architecture
authors: Julio Bermudez, Yoshio Nakamura, Amir Ebadi, Juliana Keagle, Ann Sussman, Tom Beaudoin
abstract: For seventeen centuries, basilica-plan churches have remained among Christianity’s most enduring architectural forms. Scholars have long argued that features such as bell towers, axial orientation toward the altar, upward light, noble materials, verticality, monumental scale, beauty, and figurative iconography communicate sacred meaning and shape religious experience, though these claims have remained largely grounded in historical, architectural, and theological discourse. This exploratory study recruited thirty-two committed Catholic participants to visit the Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception and Union Station, a secular control, both in Washington, DC. Using mobile eye-tracking, biometric sensing, phenomenological and perceptual reporting, and a post-visit questionnaire, the study investigated, under fully ecological conditions, which features of the basilica type shape attention, experience, and religious understanding. The findings make four contributions: (1) empirical support for longstanding claims about the basilica type, showing that its features operate as an integrated affordance-rich environment, orienting experience toward what participants identify as God; (2) demonstration that rigorous ecological investigation of sacred architectural experience is achievable without sacrificing empirical validity; (3) documentation of a three-level dissociation between aesthetic and sacred experience—pre-attentive equivalence across both buildings, semi-conscious divergence driven by figurative content, material richness, verticality, and a proposed “prelude schema,” and consciously reported differences in spirituality, connectedness, and experiential profile; and (4) a methodological framework for advancing Experimental Theological Aesthetics across architecture, liturgy, ritual, sacred art, and natural environments.

title_en: Healing After Harm: A Buddhist Contribution to Contemporary Theological Discourses on Forgiveness and Reconciliation
abstract: Taking as its departure point the urgent calls for nonviolence and reconciliation articulated by Pope Francis and Pope Leo XIV, this paper examines how Buddhist philosophy provides a systematized framework for understanding and enacting nonviolence, forgiveness, and healing after harm. While papal teachings offer a critical diagnostic of contemporary geopolitical division, militarism, and systemic inequality, a Buddhist lens deepens this discourse by illuminating the internal, psychological mechanisms required for genuine reconciliation. Drawing across Theravāda, Mahāyāna, and Tibetan traditions, this paper investigates three key dimensions: first, how Buddhist ethics conceptualizes forgiveness as an active, transformative engagement rooted in the brahmavihāras; second, how mind-training methods such as those detailed in the Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta and Lojong offer concrete tools to convert afflictive anger into compassionate understanding; and third, how these interior practices inform nonviolence education in contexts of structural injustice, demonstrating that authentic reconciliation must resist forced resolution and instead emerge through an embodied awareness of interbeing.

title_en: The Christocentric School of Rohia Monastery Around Father Nicolae Steinhardt (1912–1989) and the School of Păltiniș
abstract: The aim of the present study is to bring forward two cultural and spiritual phenomena that shaped the intellectual and religious landscapes of Romania at the end of the 20th Century and continue to influence them until nowadays. More precisely, the topic focuses on the School of Rohia Monastery gathered around the personality of the monk and man of letters Nicolae Steinhardt and the School of Păltiniș, led by the philosopher Constantin Noica. The option to treat the two phenomena in the same frame is imposed by the cultural and personal connections of the two leaders and by the similarities of the informal schools they created around them. Therefore, the research methods used in this study in order to offer a precise image of the two informal schools are the descriptive method and the comparative method. The comparative method will be used to highlight not only the similarities but, as well, the differences between the two schools and between their leaders. As this will become evident in the following lines, during the repressive regime of Ceaușescu, in the ’70s and ’80s, Steinhardt and Noica opted for a very different form of resistance: the first one chose a total refusal of adaptation and collaboration with it, while the second one accepted a formal association with it. However, both of them, in different ways, served the great ideal of culture, Father Nicolae Steinhardt from a Christian monastic setting and perspective, while the philosopher Constantin Noica from an ahistorical and purely intellectual perspective.

title_en: Does God have qualia? Some arguments in favour of the existence of divine qualia
abstract: Does God have qualia, does He know the ‘what it is like’ character of experiences? The questions run deep into the metaphysics of God as they concern concepts that most traditional theists accept with regard to God: that He is personal, loving, omniscient, omnipotent, and created the world ex nihilo . Building upon these concepts, I present four arguments in favour of the existence of divine qualia. Positing divine qualia may seem incompatible with divine simplicity, a tenet of classical theism, and the problem of emotions unworthy of God also may arise. I argue that the difficulties regarding simplicity do not stem from the existence of divine qualia per se but are related to difficulties already established in relation to simplicity. As for emotions unworthy of God, I try to show how a careful distinction between personal perspectives can offer a solution.

title_en: Life’s meaning and transcendence
abstract: This paper argues that the contemporary shift from the meaning of life to meaning in life reflects not a rejection of transcendence but a transformation in its structure. It distinguishes between absolute transcendence, which locates meaning within a comprehensive horizon beyond the situated subject, and immanent transcendence, which understands transcendence as the inexhaustibility of lived experience and interpretation. The former tends towards a third-person perspective and risks displacing the subject as the locus of meaning. The latter preserves the first-person perspective and grounds meaning in the subject’s relation to experiences, actions, and events that exceed its control. This shift also challenges the primacy of narrative identity: while narratives render actions intelligible, events reveal a more fundamental, pre-reflective dimension of subjectivity, identified here as the minimal self. Drawing on Taoist and Buddhist perspectives, particularly the concept of śūnyatā, the paper argues that meaning in life emerges through participation in a relational reality rather than through the fulfilment of an externally given purpose. Transcendence thus becomes an immanent feature of lived existence.

title_en: Are there substance dualist solutions to the non-identity problem?
journal: International Journal for Philosophy of Religion

title_en: “Can You Change the Past?” Biblical Figures, Narrative Therapy, and Faith in the Poetry of Israeli Poet Zelda
abstract: The poet Zelda (Mishkovsky), who was raised in the Chabad Hasidic tradition and was once perceived as an exceptional and “other” figure in the Israeli literary landscape, is now regarded as one of the central and most influential voices in modern Hebrew poetry. This article examines how her deep affinity for the Bible enabled her to transpose intimate psychological experiences into an archetypal-collective space, thereby establishing a defense mechanism against the personal exposure involved in the creative act. The biblical figures in her poems serve as “poetic masks” that provide her with a protective barrier, giving a name, form, and expression to complex and silenced existential content. The dialogue with these figures transforms her poetry into a therapeutic space, allowing for a renewed narrative interpretation of personal rupture. At the center of this inquiry lies the motif of the “pit” as a central metaphor for psychological rupture and trauma. Through a close reading of poems that engage in dialogue with Abraham, Joseph, Hagar, and Mephibosheth, this article delineates a spectrum of coping mechanisms and therapeutic trajectories: ranging from emotional detachment and the refusal of healing—wherein the subject remains trapped within the depths of the pit (Abraham and Hagar)—to emergence from crisis and the attainment of retroactive mending (tikkun), achieved either through the subject’s own internal resilience (Joseph) or through the active moral intervention of the lyrical speaker who rehabilitates the biblical figure’s stature (Mephibosheth). Zelda’s unique use of biblical stories in this therapeutic context draws on the Hasidic worldview in which she was raised—a worldview that remarkably aligns with contemporary psychological and bibliotherapeutic theories (such as Narrative Therapy and Logotherapy). Ultimately, the article demonstrates how the therapeutic process reflected in her poetry is intrinsically bound to faith in God—thereby presenting both a continuity of Jewish tradition and a creative contestation with biblical narratives.

title_en: God Without Theology and Theology Without God—Talmudic and Midrashic Ways of Stanislaw Lem’s Theological Thinking
abstract: This article examines, through a theological lens, the narrative landscape of Stanisław Lem—the Polish thinker and visionary author who died in 2006, leaving behind an indelible legacy in science fiction, exemplified by masterworks such as Solaris. The article begins by establishing the context, particularly focusing on the timeline of Lem’s fiction and the role of science within his narrative works. The core of the article is devoted to the concept of God and the related issue of theological thinking in Lem’s narratives. It is divided into two sections: the first explores Lem’s conception of God and theology, while the second analyses his approach to theological thinking. My intention is to argue that his theological methodology and conception of God exhibit characteristics akin to those found in Talmudic and Midrashic traditions. The text concludes with a reflection on faith from the Lemological perspective.

title_en: Persons in Relationship: African Religious and Biblical Theological Anthropology in Dialogue and Its Implications for Artificial Intelligence (AI)
authors: Martin Onukwuba, Peter Okonkwo, Michael Sunday Sasa, Ikechukwu Anthony Kanu, Michael Paul Pilani
abstract: What do African religious traditions and the Bible teach about the human person, and what might their dialogue contribute to debates about artificial intelligence (AI)? Sustained comparison between African religious sources and biblical anthropology remains rare, while existing comparisons sometimes flatten African diversity or claim agreement without examining disagreement. Using a comparative theological-hermeneutical research design based on textual and documentary analysis, conducted from a deliberately emic standpoint that reconstructs each tradition in its own terms before any external comparative category is applied, and distinguishing African religious sources from African philosophical and Christian theological interpretations, this study examines representative Yoruba, Igbo, Akan, Kikuyu, Luo, Zulu, Sotho, Tswana, and Central African Bantu sources alongside biblical texts on the image of God, human vocation, Johannine relationality, and covenantal justice. Relationality emerges as an important account of personhood across the traditions, while moral responsibility is consistently understood as extending beyond the individual to the community. However, the meaning, source, and theological grounding of relationality differ substantially, and the traditions diverge on revelation, ritual authority, freedom, sin, salvation, and life after death. The comparative anthropology is the article’s main contribution. AI implications follow as a secondary application, proposing relational dignity, shared accountability, epistemic humility, and attention to vulnerable people as principles for responsible AI governance.

title_en: Gratitude to God in the Face of Adversity and Illness in Christianity and Islam
abstract: The conventional understanding of gratitude assumes that feeling grateful is reserved for joyous times. However, gratefulness during severe adversity is also documented. This paper focuses on this second phenomenon, examining experiences of gratitude toward God among Christian and Muslim parents of critically ill or disabled children. The ethnographic literature on this topic remains scarce. The goal of this paper is to read the few details this ethnographic literature offers in conjunction with Christian and Muslim theology on gratitude and adversity. Such an interpretive exercise sets out the theological resources these believers may draw upon. Our analysis reveals that reasons for their gratitude fall into two main categories: feeling grateful toward God despite adversity, or because of adversity. The essay compares these experiences in Christianity and Islam to highlight those key conceptual differences that emerge from the material. It also holds that the experience of gratitude towards God under conditions of suffering might partly destabilize the conventional philosophical model of gratitude. Overall, the material surveyed maps the range of meanings illness holds for some Christian and Muslim parents, offering valuable insights not only to theologians and philosophers of religion, but also to clinicians and chaplains.

title_en: Meaning, desire, and the limits of atheism
abstract: This paper defends a theistic framing of the problem of life’s meaning, albeit one which is intended to be compatible with a kind of naturalism. It makes explicit the significance of desire for an understanding of the issues at hand and draws out some implications for the question of the limits of atheism.

title_en: The human project or what difference would God make?
abstract: Many people believe that, without any God or something similarly ‘transcendent’, human life would be meaningless. I oppose this position. In its most popular form, it supposes that meaning accrues because our mundane life is merely a prelude – a time of trial, to decide the character of our life in the hereafter. When probed, this approach involves a number of implausible corollaries. More abstract approaches suggest that meaningfulness results from human contributions to a larger project, the fulfilment of some divine (or transcendent) scheme for the universe. That idea is more promising, but it fails to recognize the possibility of a larger – ‘human’ – project to which our lives may also contribute, and that from such contributions can arise significance. This possibility is suggested by John Dewey, and traces of it can be found in a number of insightful poets, Herbert, Wordsworth, and Whitman. Finally, I rebut the thought that, without something transcendent, there can be no values.

Quantised Spacetime and the Case against Actual Infinities
The Value of Becoming Actual: Antinatalism, Cosmic Meaning, and Ontological Natal Permissibilism
authors: Ana Maria Correa Moreira da Silva, Leandro Prade Nadaletti
abstract: David Benatar’s antinatalism holds that coming into existence is always a harm and that procreation is therefore morally impermissible. This article develops a non-theistic alternative to a recent supernaturalist response to Benatar offered by Wakeman and Launonen. It defends ontological natal permissibilism: the view that actualizing a possible person as a perspectival subject is a defeasible prima facie good, and that this good can contribute to the moral permissibility of procreation when the expected conditions of life do not defeat it. The argument does not defend demographic pronatalism, a duty to reproduce, or the maximization of births. It instead challenges the priority Benatar gives to harm-avoidance by arguing that non-existence is not peace, protection, or safety, but the absence of a subject. Drawing on debates over cosmic meaning, Christian universalism, eternalism, and the Block Universe, the article distinguishes between physical and perspectival permanence. Mere inscription in spacetime does not generate value, since stones, collisions, and horrors also occur. Value arises when actuality includes conscious relation to reality, embodied presence, and world-contact. Ontological joy names the non-hedonic value of becoming actual as a possible perspective. Extreme suffering may defeat procreative permissibility, but it does not establish that birth is always only the imposition of harm.

title_en: Atheism, evolution, and meaning
abstract: In this paper, I argue that meaning of the main kinds associated with human life can be described and illuminatingly discussed by atheists who reject all things religious and embrace evolution. Indeed, by considering the different forms evolution can take and with sensitivity to how distinctive meaning-related facts emerge at different stages of macroscale human development and also to the fact that meaning itself evolves, atheists are in a position to show that the evolutionary considerations available to them, rather than an obstacle to a robust and satisfying account of meaning, can be its source.

title_en: Reconciling feminist critiques and classic theories of atonement
abstract: Work on atonement is fractured around how to respond to feminist critiques of classic atonement theories (such as satisfaction, moral exemplar, and penal substitution theories). Feminist and womanist scholars have levelled various critiques of these theories: the theories glorify sadomasochistic suffering, they encourage passivity in the face of suffering, and they are complicit in the oppression, victimization, and disempowerment of women in part because they legitimize patterns of oppression. Defenders of the classic theories have given various replies to these critiques, but these replies leave many feeling the heart of the critiques hasn’t really been addressed. In this paper, I aim to mend this fracture. I believe there is wisdom and insight on both sides of this dispute and that reflecting more carefully on a certain strand of feminist critique will present tools for mending. I develop a version of a feminist critique inspired by comments in several feminist critics of atonement theories – most notably Elizabeth Schussler Fiorenza. According to the critique I develop, the classic theories, together with Christian moral norms to imitate Christ, imply some version of the problematic attitudes mentioned above. This critique avoids the main objections to other feminist critiques. I then examine the notion of imitation and argue that, properly understood, the norm of imitating Christ (together with the classic atonement theories) does not have the problematic implications. Indeed, the norm and classic theories imply that imitating Christ by aiming at reconciliation among people requires rejecting the problematic attitudes.

title_en: Religious antinatalism: a rare breed
abstract: This article examines the relationship between religion and antinatalism – the view that it is wrong to create new sentient beings. Many people reject antinatalism on religious grounds. In this paper, I respond to such a rejection. First, I argue that antinatalism is not logically incompatible with theism. Second, I consider the pronatalist features of some religious traditions – those of Judaism, Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism. These include religious injunctions to procreate, imitatio Dei , and preservation of the religious community. I also show the limits of these pronatalist features. Third, I provide some examples of religious antinatalist thinking in the four surveyed religions. Finally, I say something about why many religions should be more antinatalist than they are. I do this by showing how central concepts – such as reducing suffering in Buddhism and original sin and hell in Christianity – provide compelling support for antinatalism.

title_en: A Review of the Functions and Properties of the Bhavaṅga-Citta: Reply to Sean Smith
Divine simplicity as symmetric parthood
abstract: Taken at face value, the doctrine of divine simplicity (DDS) says that God lacks proper parts, but the doctrine is also often formulated as a thesis identifying God with all his parts. The two formulations are not generally equivalent – on some plausible mereological theories, something can lack proper parts by being a part of all its (possibly distinct) parts. Thus, the DDS can be alternatively formulated as a thesis saying that God is part of all his parts – call this the symmetry formulation. The symmetry formulation is viable as a thesis about God’s relation to his attributes, because instantiation can plausibly be modelled as parthood. Moreover, the symmetry formulation retains the usual motivations for divine simplicity coming from the doctrines of aseity, transcendence, immutability, and unity. The symmetry formulation also addresses common objections to divine simplicity regarding distinctness in God’s attributes and those coming from modal collapse arguments.
